payload.body: The maximum flow derivative (MFD) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak rate of change of glottal flow within a glottal cycle, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. Given the glottal flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, MFD is computed as the maximum magnitude of the first derivative (or first difference) of g within each pitch-synchronous cycle, max |g(n+1) - g(n)|, then aggregated across cycles by the median or mean over the analyzed frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the derivative operator — first difference or finite difference over the sampled flow, (4) the normalization choice — absolute units (volume per sample interval) or relative to the cycle's maximum flow, and (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high MFD marks a sharp glottal closure (pressed, spiky phonation) and a low MFD marks a gradual closure (breathy phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside jitter, shimmer, and the phase quotients. payload.body: Formant dispersion (D) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the mean spacing between the first three formant frequencies of a voiced segment, reported in hertz as D = (F3 - F1) / 2, equivalently the mean of (F2 - F1) and (F3 - F2). Given formant estimates F1, F2, F3 per analysis frame, D is computed per frame from the frame's three lowest formant frequencies and aggregated across the voiced segment by mean (and, where maintained, standard deviation). Its parameters are: (1) the formant frequency estimates F1, F2, F3 per analysis frame — the vocal-tract resonances located by formant tracking, (2) the dispersion operator — (F3 - F1)/2 or the mean of consecutive spacings, (3) the cross-frame aggregation (mean, standard deviation, or median) over the analyzed voiced segment. A larger dispersion indicates a shorter, stiffer vocal tract (child-like or laryngectomized voice) and a smaller dispersion a longer tract, with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in hertz and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside jitter, shimmer, the phase quotients, and the noise ratios. payload.body: Peak flow is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak glottal flow within each glottal cycle, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. Given the glottal flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the peak flow is computed as the maximum of g within each pitch-synchronous cycle, max_n g(n), then aggregated across cycles by the median or mean over the analyzed frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the peak operator — the maximum of the sampled flow within the cycle, (4) the normalization choice — absolute flow units or relative to the cycle's mean flow, and (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high peak flow marks a leaky, breathy source with a large open-phase flow excursion and a low peak flow a pressed source with a tightly modulated pulse, with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside the maximum flow derivative, voice onset time, jitter, shimmer, and the phase quotients. payload.body: The glottal closure instant (GCI) is a voice-quality parameter locating the point of glottal closure within each glottal cycle: the instant at which the glottal airflow returns to baseline and the closed phase begins. In the pinned sense it is estimated from the glottal flow waveform (glottogram) g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking: within each pitch-synchronous cycle, the GCI is the time point of the cycle's minimum glottal flow - the flow trough returning to baseline - equivalently the point where the first derivative of the flow crosses zero from negative to positive. It is reported per cycle as a time point and as the normalized GCI (nGCI), the difference between successive closure instants divided by the intervening fundamental period, a dimensionless ratio with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation: a prolonged nGCI marks increased glottal closure as in spastic or hyperfunctional dysphonia, a shortened nGCI a breathy, insufficiently closed source.
